title: Diagnosing Humidity in a 3-Ton A/C System: Heat-Gain Calculation, UV Light Impact, and Filtration Upgrades

locations.name: Attic (air handler)
locations.basis: Explicit mention of the air handler being in the attic

summary: The video documents a humidity problem following a new air conditioner installation. The host evaluates whether the system is correctly sized, performs a heat gain check, and confirms the unit is a three-ton system appropriate for the building’s insulation and envelope. It then examines how a smart thermostat and a UV germicidal light may be influencing humidity and fan behavior, identifying unintended consequences that can worsen moisture control. The solution centers on improving filtration and airflow: upgrading to a high-density, five-inch pleated filter, modifying the return duct to accommodate the larger filter housing, sealing the air path, and adjusting the thermostat to run the fan during cooling to enhance dehumidification. The UV feature is noted to be limited in addressing allergens, reinforcing filtration as the key strategy for reducing humidity and allergens.
topics: Building envelope factors (roof, walls, sun exposure, trees)
Continuous fan operation and UV light interaction
Return duct modification for filter housing

sections.title: Assess system size and heat gain
sections.description: The speaker introduces extreme humidity after a new install and attributes it to potential oversizing. He explains the importance of a heat gain calculation to determine the correct tonnage and checks the attic-installed unit and envelope (noting the roof has no insulation and walls are concrete block) to see if the three-ton system is appropriate.

sections.title: Thermostat behavior and UV light impact
concepts: Narrowing humidity setpoints and operating window
Humidity dynamics when the thermostat turns off
UV germicidal light and its effect on airflow
Fan operation and how it influences moisture
sections.description: Discussion shifts to how a smart thermostat can create humidity swings if the system short-cycles or is left off during the day. The host also identifies a UV light in the air handler that is designed to reduce germs but may cause the fan to run constantly, affecting humidity dynamics.

sections.title: Filtration upgrades and air path modifications
concepts: Return duct modification for filter housing
Foil tape sealing and cover plate installation
sections.description: The video demonstrates upgrading filtration by replacing a dirty 1-inch filter with a high-density five-inch pleated filter, installing a dedicated filter cabinet in the return air path, sealing the assembly with foil tape, and reattaching the return. The contractor Terry McClellan performs the cutout, filter installation, and sealing while the host notes the thermostat setting adjustment to improve dehumidification.

featured_techniques.technique: Heat gain calculation to determine proper system size (tons)

Identify unintended consequences of UV germicidal light on humidity and continuous fan
Upgrade filtration from 1-inch to 5-inch pleated filter for better air quality
Modify return duct to accommodate higher-efficiency filter housing
Seal air path with foil tape and install cover plate for airtight filter installation
Configure thermostat to run the fan in cooling mode to improve dehumidification
Educate on UV light limitations for allergy control and emphasize filtration
